Use in the mathematics_lean domain, when a proof needs machine-checked verification but installing Lean/Mathlib locally is undesirable, or when translating informal proofs into formally verified Lean 4 code checked in the cloud. (project)

commands.name: citation-manager
commands.description: Manage BibTeX citations including DOI-to-BibTeX conversion, metadata extraction, validation, and deduplication. Use when building reference lists, converting DOIs to citations, or validating existing .bib files. (project)

commands.name: critical-analysis
commands.description: Evaluate research quality using frameworks like GRADE, bias detection, and logical analysis. Use when assessing paper quality, evaluating claims, or reviewing evidence strength. (project)

commands.name: data-analysis
commands.description: Conduct exploratory data analysis and statistical testing with test selection guidance. Use when exploring datasets, selecting statistical tests, performing power analysis, or preparing results for publication. (project)

commands.name: grant-writing
commands.description: Write research grant proposals with guidance for NSF, NIH, DARPA, and other agencies. Use when preparing grant applications, developing research plans, or writing broader impacts statements. (project)

commands.name: hypothesis-generation
commands.description: Formulate research hypotheses using structured frameworks. Use when developing research questions, designing experiments, or planning studies with testable predictions. (project)

commands.name: literature-review
commands.description: Conduct systematic literature reviews using a structured workflow. Use when starting a new research project, surveying a field, or documenting related work for a paper. (project)

commands.name: paper-finder
commands.description: Find and search for academic papers using the paper-finder service. Use when conducting literature review, searching for related work, finding baseline papers, or looking for methodology references. (project)

commands.name: paper-writer
commands.description: Write academic papers from experiment results using LaTeX. Use when experiments are complete and REPORT.md exists, when asked to write a paper, or when generating publication-ready documents in NeurIPS style. (project)

commands.name: peer-review
commands.description: Conduct structured manuscript reviews with section-by-section checklists and constructive feedback. Use when reviewing papers before submission, providing feedback to colleagues, or preparing reviewer responses. (project)

commands.name: research-brainstorming
commands.description: Creative ideation for research using structured methods like SCAMPER, morphological analysis, and cross-domain analogies. Use when generating research ideas, exploring new directions, or overcoming creative blocks. (project)

commands.name: deep-research
commands.description: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. (dynamic workflow)

commands.name: design
commands.description: Grant or revoke Claude agent access to your Design projects

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts

commands.name: doctor

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

commands.name: built-in-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:deep-research
commands.description: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docs
commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: import-memory
commands.description: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: morning
commands.description: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: skill-creator
commands.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

# Planning: Attention Entropy as a Predictor of Hallucination

Written before any model was run. Deviations are logged at the bottom.

## Motivation & Novelty Assessment

### Why This Research Matters
LLMs state wrong facts in the same fluent register as right ones. Detectors that need
only a single forward pass and no external knowledge are attractive because they are
cheap enough to run on every response. Attention maps are available for free in that
pass; if their dispersion (entropy) tracks factual error, it is a nearly zero-cost
warning signal and also says something about *how* a model behaves when it lacks the fact.

### Gap in Existing Work
(The resource-finding stage was skipped for this run, so there is no
`literature_review.md`; this is from my own knowledge of the area.)
- Output-distribution methods (token likelihood, predictive/semantic entropy,
  SelfCheckGPT) use logits or multiple samples, not attention.
- Hidden-state probes (SAPLMA; INSIDE/EigenScore; Orgad et al. 2024) use residual activations.
- Attention-based detectors exist but use other statistics: Lookback Lens (ratio of
  attention on context vs. generated tokens, RAG setting), LLM-Check (attention kernel
  log-determinants), Yuksekgonul et al. 2024 (attention *mass* on constraint tokens).
- What is missing is a direct, controlled test of the simple claim "attention is more
  diffuse when hallucinating": a stated effect size by layer, a classifier restricted to
  layer-wise entropy, explicit control of the sequence-length confound (entropy is
  bounded by log n), and a per-domain breakdown.

### Our Novel Contribution
A pre-specified test of three quantitative claims (15-30% higher late-layer entropy;
AUROC > 0.75 from layer-wise entropy alone; biography > science ordering) on two
open-weight model families across five knowledge domains, with length controls and
logit baselines.

### Experiment Justification
- E1 (effect size by layer): directly tests the "15-30% higher in final 3 layers" claim.
- E2 (entropy-only logistic classifier): tests "AUROC > 0.75".
- E3 (per-domain AUROC + cross-domain transfer): tests the domain-ordering claim and
  whether the signal is domain-general.
- E4 (controls/baselines): length-only, token-likelihood, and combined models; tells
  us whether entropy carries signal beyond trivial confounds and beyond logits.
- E5 (robustness): second model family, alternative labels, first-token vs
  answer-averaged features, per-head features.

## Research Question
In closed-book short-answer QA, is self-attention entropy at answer-generation time
higher for hallucinated (factually wrong) answers than for correct ones, by how much in
the last 3 layers, and how well does a logistic classifier on per-layer entropy detect
hallucination, overall and per domain?

## Hypothesis Decomposition
- H1: mean attention entropy over the final 3 layers is 15-30% higher for hallucinated
  than for correct answers. Supported only if the relative difference (and its 95% CI)
  lies in/overlaps that band with the right sign.
- H2: logistic regression on per-layer entropy features only reaches cross-validated
  AUROC > 0.75 (pooled over domains). Supported if the 95% CI lower bound > 0.75;
  "borderline" if the CI straddles 0.75.
- H3: within-domain AUROC is highest for biography and lowest for science.

Variables. Independent: answer correctness (hallucinated vs factual), domain, layer,
model. Dependent: attention entropy; detector AUROC.

## Proposed Methodology

### Models (local, open weights; attention maps are required, so no API models)
- Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (28 layers x 28 heads) - primary.
- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (32 layers x 32 heads) - replication.
fp16, greedy decoding, max 24 new tokens, chat template with a fixed system prompt.

### Data (1,500 questions per domain, seed 42, 7,500 per model)
| Domain | Source |
|---|---|
| biography | PopQA relations occupation / place of birth / father / mother |
| geography | PopQA country / capital / capital of |
| creative works | PopQA author / director / producer / screenwriter / composer |
| science | SciQ (train split, question + correct answer, no support passage) |
| general trivia | TriviaQA rc.nocontext validation |

Known confound: science and trivia come from different datasets than the three PopQA
domains, so "domain" is partly "dataset/question style". Reported as a limitation.

### Labels
- Primary: reference-based LLM judge (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, a different and larger
  model than either subject, temperature 0) given question, gold answers, model answer;
  outputs CORRECT / INCORRECT / ABSTAIN.
- Secondary (robustness): normalized string containment of any gold alias.
- Abstentions/refusals are excluded from the hallucinated-vs-factual comparison and counted.
- Rationale for a judge as primary: SciQ gold answers are free-form phrases where
  string match would produce false "hallucinations" specifically in the science domain,
  biasing H3. No commercial API key is available in this environment, hence a local judge.

### Features
One teacher-forced forward pass over prompt + generated answer with eager attention.
For every layer l, head h, and each position p that *produces* an answer token:
H = -sum_j a_pj log a_pj (nats). Aggregations saved per example:
- `ans_mean`: mean over answer-producing positions (primary; "during generation").
- `first`: position producing the first answer token (depends on the prompt only, so
  it cannot leak answer length).
Layer feature = mean over heads -> L features per example. Also normalized entropy
H / log(n_p) with n_p = number of attended positions.

### Experimental Steps
1. Build the 7,500-question set; 2. generate answers; 3. extract entropy + logit stats;
4. judge; 5. analysis E1-E5.

### Baselines / controls
- Chance (0.5); length-only (prompt tokens, answer tokens).
- Logit baselines: mean token negative log-likelihood, max token NLL, mean predictive
  entropy of the next-token distribution, first-token probability.
- Entropy + length; entropy + logit (does attention add anything?).
- Per-head entropy (L*H features, L2-regularized) as an upper bound for entropy-only.

### Evaluation Metrics
- E1: relative difference of means (halluc - factual)/factual for the last-3-layer mean,
  percentile bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples); Cohen's d; Mann-Whitney U. Per-layer
  d with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR across layers. Same after residualizing entropy on
  log prompt length and log answer length (and for normalized entropy).
- E2-E4: AUROC, out-of-fold predictions from 5-fold stratified CV repeated 5 times
  (standardization fit inside folds, default C=1), bootstrap 95% CI on pooled
  out-of-fold scores. AUPRC reported as secondary.
- E3: within-domain CV AUROC per domain with CI; bootstrap test of
  AUROC(biography) - AUROC(science); 5x5 train-domain -> test-domain transfer matrix.
- alpha = 0.05.

## Expected Outcomes
Support: +15-30% late-layer entropy, pooled AUROC CI above 0.75, biography top /
science bottom in both models. Refutation: effect of other size/sign, AUROC CI below
0.75, or a different ordering. A likely partial outcome is a real but small entropy
shift with moderate AUROC that is partly explained by length.

## Timeline
Setup/data 30 min; generation+extraction 45 min; judging 20 min; analysis 60 min;
report 40 min.

## Potential Challenges
- Disk nearly full on /data (6 GB): venv uses symlinks to the uv cache; only cached
  models; outputs kept small (per-example L x H float16 arrays).
- Entropy/length confound: handled by normalized and residualized variants and the
  length-only baseline.
- Class imbalance differs by domain (PopQA is long-tail, mostly wrong): AUROC is
  prevalence-free; base rates reported.
- Judge errors: quantify agreement with string match; rerun headline numbers on
  string-match labels.

## Success Criteria
All three sub-hypotheses receive a clear supported / not supported / mixed verdict
with CIs, on both models, with the controls above.

## Deviations from plan
(filled in during execution)

# Planning: Attention Entropy as a Predictor of Hallucination

Written before any model was run. Deviations are logged at the bottom.

## Motivation & Novelty Assessment

### Why This Research Matters
LLMs state wrong facts in the same fluent register as right ones. Detectors that need
only a single forward pass and no external knowledge are attractive because they are
cheap enough to run on every response. Attention maps are available for free in that
pass; if their dispersion (entropy) tracks factual error, it is a nearly zero-cost
warning signal and also says something about *how* a model behaves when it lacks the fact.

### Gap in Existing Work
(The resource-finding stage was skipped for this run, so there is no
`literature_review.md`; this is from my own knowledge of the area.)
- Output-distribution methods (token likelihood, predictive/semantic entropy,
  SelfCheckGPT) use logits or multiple samples, not attention.
- Hidden-state probes (SAPLMA; INSIDE/EigenScore; Orgad et al. 2024) use residual activations.
- Attention-based detectors exist but use other statistics: Lookback Lens (ratio of
  attention on context vs. generated tokens, RAG setting), LLM-Check (attention kernel
  log-determinants), Yuksekgonul et al. 2024 (attention *mass* on constraint tokens).
- What is missing is a direct, controlled test of the simple claim "attention is more
  diffuse when hallucinating": a stated effect size by layer, a classifier restricted to
  layer-wise entropy, explicit control of the sequence-length confound (entropy is
  bounded by log n), and a per-domain breakdown.

### Our Novel Contribution
A pre-specified test of three quantitative claims (15-30% higher late-layer entropy;
AUROC > 0.75 from layer-wise entropy alone; biography > science ordering) on two
open-weight model families across five knowledge domains, with length controls and
logit baselines.

### Experiment Justification
- E1 (effect size by layer): directly tests the "15-30% higher in final 3 layers" claim.
- E2 (entropy-only logistic classifier): tests "AUROC > 0.75".
- E3 (per-domain AUROC + cross-domain transfer): tests the domain-ordering claim and
  whether the signal is domain-general.
- E4 (controls/baselines): length-only, token-likelihood, and combined models; tells
  us whether entropy carries signal beyond trivial confounds and beyond logits.
- E5 (robustness): second model family, alternative labels, first-token vs
  answer-averaged features, per-head features.

## Research Question
In closed-book short-answer QA, is self-attention entropy at answer-generation time
higher for hallucinated (factually wrong) answers than for correct ones, by how much in
the last 3 layers, and how well does a logistic classifier on per-layer entropy detect
hallucination, overall and per domain?

## Hypothesis Decomposition
- H1: mean attention entropy over the final 3 layers is 15-30% higher for hallucinated
  than for correct answers. Supported only if the relative difference (and its 95% CI)
  lies in/overlaps that band with the right sign.
- H2: logistic regression on per-layer entropy features only reaches cross-validated
  AUROC > 0.75 (pooled over domains). Supported if the 95% CI lower bound > 0.75;
  "borderline" if the CI straddles 0.75.
- H3: within-domain AUROC is highest for biography and lowest for science.

Variables. Independent: answer correctness (hallucinated vs factual), domain, layer,
model. Dependent: attention entropy; detector AUROC.

| Domain | Source |
|---|---|

| geography | PopQA country / capital / capital of |
| creative works | PopQA author / director / producer / screenwriter / composer |
| science | SciQ (train split, question + correct answer, no support passage) |
| general trivia | TriviaQA rc.nocontext validation |

domains, so "domain" is partly "dataset/question style". Reported as a limitation.

  model than either subject, temperature 0) given question, gold answers, model answer;
  outputs CORRECT / INCORRECT / ABSTAIN.
- Secondary (robustness): normalized string containment of any gold alias.
- Abstentions/refusals are excluded from the hallucinated-vs-factual comparison and counted.
- Rationale for a judge as primary: SciQ gold answers are free-form phrases where
  string match would produce false "hallucinations" specifically in the science domain,

One teacher-forced forward pass over prompt + generated answer with eager attention.

"""Build the 5-domain closed-book QA set (1,500 questions per domain, seed 42).

Output: datasets/processed/questions.jsonl with fields
  qid, domain, source, relation, question, gold (list of acceptable answers)
"""
import json
import os
import re

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

SEED = 42
N_PER_DOMAIN = 1500
RAW = "datasets/raw"
OUT = "datasets/processed/questions.jsonl"

POPQA_DOMAINS = {
    "biography": ["occupation", "place of birth", "father", "mother"],
    "geography": ["country", "capital", "capital of"],
    "creative_works": ["author", "director", "producer", "screenwriter", "composer"],
}


def main():
    rng = np.random.RandomState(SEED)
    rows = []

    pop = pd.read_csv(f"{RAW}/PopQA/test.tsv", sep="\t")
    for domain, props in POPQA_DOMAINS.items():
        sub = pop[pop.prop.isin(props)]
        assert len(sub) >= N_PER_DOMAIN, (domain, len(sub))
        sub = sub.sample(N_PER_DOMAIN, random_state=rng)
        for r in sub.itertuples():
            rows.append(dict(qid=f"popqa-{r.id}", domain=domain, source="PopQA", relation=r.prop,
                             question=r.question, gold=json.loads(r.possible_answers)))

    sci = pd.read_parquet(f"{RAW}/sciq/data/train-00000-of-00001.parquet")
    # Keep self-contained questions: must end with '?' (drops cloze-style fragments).
    sci = sci[sci.question.str.strip().str.endswith("?")].drop_duplicates("question")
    sci = sci.sample(N_PER_DOMAIN, random_state=rng)
    for i, r in zip(sci.index, sci.itertuples()):
        rows.append(dict(qid=f"sciq-{i}", domain="science", source="SciQ", relation="",
                         question=r.question.strip(), gold=[r.correct_answer.strip()]))

    tq = pd.read_parquet(f"{RAW}/trivia_qa/rc.nocontext/validation-00000-of-00001.parquet")
    tq = tq.drop_duplicates("question").sample(N_PER_DOMAIN, random_state=rng)
    for r in tq.itertuples():
        gold = list(dict.fromkeys([r.answer["value"], *r.answer["aliases"]]))
        rows.append(dict(qid=f"tqa-{r.question_id}", domain="trivia", source="TriviaQA", relation="",
                         question=re.sub(r"\s+", " ", r.question).strip(), gold=gold))

    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(OUT), exist_ok=True)
    with open(OUT, "w") as f:
        for r in rows:
            f.write(json.dumps(r, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    assert df.qid.is_unique and df.question.str.len().min() > 5
    print(df.groupby(["domain", "source"]).size())
    print(df.groupby("domain").relation.value_counts().to_string())
    print("question chars:", df.question.str.len().describe().round(1).to_dict())
    print(df.groupby("domain").head(2)[["domain", "question", "gold"]].to_string())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Generate closed-book answers and extract attention-entropy + logit features.

For each question:
  1. greedy-decode a short answer (chat template, fixed system prompt);
  2. run ONE teacher-forced pass over prompt+answer with eager attention;
  3. for every layer/head, compute the Shannon entropy (nats) of the attention row of
     each position that *produces* an answer token.

Saved to results/features/<tag>.npz (arrays indexed like results/model_outputs/<tag>.jsonl):
  ent_ans   (N, L, H) mean entropy over answer-producing positions
  ent_first (N, L, H) entropy at the position producing the first answer token
  nent_ans, nent_first: same, each row divided by log(#attended positions)
  logit stats and lengths in the jsonl.
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import time

import numpy as np
import torch
from tqdm import tqdm
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

SYSTEM = ("You are a knowledgeable assistant. Answer the question with only the short answer "
          "(a name or a few words). Do not explain. Always give your best guess.")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--model", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--tag", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--data", default="datasets/processed/questions.jsonl")
    ap.add_argument("--batch_size", type=int, default=32)
    ap.add_argument("--max_new_tokens", type=int, default=24)
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=0)
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    np.random.seed(args.seed)
    qs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(args.data)]
    if args.limit:
        qs = qs[:: max(1, len(qs) // args.limit)][: args.limit]

    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(args.model)
    tok.padding_side = "left"
    if tok.pad_token is None:
        tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        args.model, dtype=torch.float16, attn_implementation="eager").cuda().eval()
    L, H = model.config.num_hidden_layers, model.config.num_attention_heads
    print(f"{args.model}: L={L} H={H}", flush=True)
    stop_ids = {tok.eos_token_id, *[i for i in tok.convert_tokens_to_ids(["<|eot_id|>", "<|im_end|>"])
                                    if i is not None and i != tok.unk_token_id]}

    os.makedirs("results/features", exist_ok=True)
    os.makedirs("results/model_outputs", exist_ok=True)
    feats = {k: [] for k in ["ent_ans", "ent_first", "nent_ans", "nent_first"]}
    records = []
    t0 = time.time()
    # Sort by length so batches need little padding; original order restored at the end.
    prompts = [tok.apply_chat_template(
        [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": q["question"]}],
        tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) for q in qs]
    p_ids = [tok(p, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids for p in prompts]
    order = np.argsort([len(x) for x in p_ids], kind="stable")

    for b in tqdm(range(0, len(order), args.batch_size), mininterval=30):
        idx = order[b: b + args.batch_size]
        batch = [p_ids[i] for i in idx]
        T = max(map(len, batch))
        ids = torch.full((len(batch), T), tok.pad_token_id)
        mask = torch.zeros((len(batch), T), dtype=torch.long)
        for j, x in enumerate(batch):
            ids[j, T - len(x):] = torch.tensor(x)
            mask[j, T - len(x):] = 1
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = model.generate(input_ids=ids.cuda(), attention_mask=mask.cuda(), do_sample=False,
                                 max_new_tokens=args.max_new_tokens, pad_token_id=tok.pad_token_id,
                                 eos_token_id=list(stop_ids))
        gens = []
        for j in range(len(batch)):
            g = out[j, T:].tolist()
            cut = next((k for k, t in enumerate(g) if t in stop_ids), len(g))
            gens.append(g[:cut])

        # Teacher-forced pass over prompt + answer (answer tokens only, no EOS).
        full = [batch[j] + gens[j] for j in range(len(batch))]
        T2 = max(map(len, full))
        ids2 = torch.full((len(full), T2), tok.pad_token_id)
        mask2 = torch.zeros((len(full), T2), dtype=torch.long)
        for j, x in enumerate(full):
            ids2[j, T2 - len(x):] = torch.tensor(x)
            mask2[j, T2 - len(x):] = 1
        with torch.no_grad():
            o = model(input_ids=ids2.cuda(), attention_mask=mask2.cuda(), output_attentions=True)
            # (L, B, H, T2): entropy of every attention row.
            ent = torch.stack([-(a.float() * torch.log(a.float().clamp_min(1e-12))).sum(-1)
                               for a in o.attentions])
            if b == 0:  # sanity: rows are probability distributions
                s = o.attentions[-1].float().sum(-1)[mask2.bool().cuda()[:, None, :].expand(-1, H, -1)]
                assert (s - 1).abs().max() < 2e-2, s
            logp = torch.log_softmax(o.logits.float(), -1)
            pent = -(logp.exp() * logp).sum(-1)  # predictive entropy per position (B, T2)

        for j, qi in enumerate(idx):
            P, m, n = len(batch[j]), len(gens[j]), len(full[j])
            off = T2 - n
            rec = dict(qs[qi], answer=tok.decode(gens[j], skip_special_tokens=True).strip(),
                       n_prompt=P, n_answer=m, order=int(qi))
            if m == 0:
                for k in feats:
                    feats[k].append(np.full((L, H), np.nan, dtype=np.float32))
                records.append(rec)
                continue
            pos = torch.arange(P - 1, P + m - 1, device=ent.device)  # unpadded positions producing answer tokens
            e = ent[:, j, :, off + pos]                               # (L, H, m)
            ne = e / torch.log((pos + 1).float())                     # row at position p attends to p+1 tokens
            feats["ent_ans"].append(e.mean(-1).cpu().numpy())
            feats["ent_first"].append(e[..., 0].cpu().numpy())
            feats["nent_ans"].append(ne.mean(-1).cpu().numpy())
            feats["nent_first"].append(ne[..., 0].cpu().numpy())
            tgt = torch.tensor(gens[j], device=ent.device)
            nll = -logp[j, off + pos, tgt]
            pe = pent[j, off + pos]
            rec.update(nll_mean=nll.mean().item(), nll_max=nll.max().item(), nll_first=nll[0].item(),
                       pent_mean=pe.mean().item(), pent_max=pe.max().item(), pent_first=pe[0].item())
            records.append(rec)
        del o, ent, logp, pent

    inv = np.argsort([r["order"] for r in records])
    records = [records[i] for i in inv]
    with open(f"results/model_outputs/{args.tag}.jsonl", "w") as f:
        for r in records:
            f.write(json.dumps(r, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    np.savez_compressed(f"results/features/{args.tag}.npz",
                        **{k: np.stack(v)[inv].astype(np.float16) for k, v in feats.items()})
    print(f"done {len(records)} examples in {time.time() - t0:.0f}s; "
          f"empty answers: {sum(r['n_answer'] == 0 for r in records)}", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

SYSTEM = ("You are a knowledgeable assistant. Answer the question with only the short answer "
          "(a name or a few words). Do not explain. Always give your best guess.")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--model", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--tag", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--data", default="datasets/processed/questions.jsonl")
    ap.add_argument("--batch_size", type=int, default=32)
    ap.add_argument("--max_new_tokens", type=int, default=24)
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=0)
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    np.random.seed(args.seed)
    qs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(args.data)]
    if args.limit:
        qs = qs[:: max(1, len(qs) // args.limit)][: args.limit]

    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(args.model)
    tok.padding_side = "left"
    if tok.pad_token is None:
        tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        args.model, dtype=torch.float16, attn_implementation="eager").cuda().eval()
    L, H = model.config.num_hidden_layers, model.config.num_attention_heads
    print(f"{args.model}: L={L} H={H}", flush=True)
    stop_ids = {tok.eos_token_id, *[i for i in tok.convert_tokens_to_ids(["<|eot_id|>", "<|im_end|>"])
                                    if i is not None and i != tok.unk_token_id]}

    os.makedirs("results/features", exist_ok=True)
    os.makedirs("results/model_outputs", exist_ok=True)
    feats = {k: [] for k in ["ent_ans", "ent_first", "nent_ans", "nent_first"]}
    records = []
    t0 = time.time()
    # Sort by length so batches need little padding; original order restored at the end.
    prompts = [tok.apply_chat_template(
        [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": q["question"]}],
        tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) for q in qs]
    p_ids = [tok(p, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids for p in prompts]
    order = np.argsort([len(x) for x in p_ids], kind="stable")

    for b in tqdm(range(0, len(order), args.batch_size), mininterval=30):
        idx = order[b: b + args.batch_size]
        batch = [p_ids[i] for i in idx]
        T = max(map(len, batch))
        ids = torch.full((len(batch), T), tok.pad_token_id)
        mask = torch.zeros((len(batch), T), dtype=torch.long)
        for j, x in enumerate(batch):
            ids[j, T - len(x):] = torch.tensor(x)
            mask[j, T - len(x):] = 1
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = model.generate(input_ids=ids.cuda(), attention_mask=mask.cuda(), do_sample=False,
                                 max_new_tokens=args.max_new_tokens, pad_token_id=tok.pad_token_id,
                                 eos_token_id=list(stop_ids))
        gens = []
        for j in range(len(batch)):
            g = out[j, T:].tolist()
            cut = next((k for k, t in enumerate(g) if t in stop_ids), len(g))
            gens.append(g[:cut])

        # Teacher-forced pass over prompt + answer (answer tokens only, no EOS).
        full = [batch[j] + gens[j] for j in range(len(batch))]
        T2 = max(map(len, full))
        ids2 = torch.full((len(full), T2), tok.pad_token_id)
        mask2 = torch.zeros((len(full), T2), dtype=torch.long)
        for j, x in enumerate(full):
            ids2[j, T2 - len(x):] = torch.tensor(x)
            mask2[j, T2 - len(x):] = 1
        with torch.no_grad():
            o = model(input_ids=ids2.cuda(), attention_mask=mask2.cuda(), output_attentions=True)
            # (L, B, H, T2): entropy of every attention row.
            ent = torch.stack([-(a.float() * torch.log(a.float().clamp_min(1e-12))).sum(-1)
                               for a in o.attentions])
            if b == 0:  # sanity: rows are probability distributions
                s = o.attentions[-1].float().sum(-1)[mask2.bool().cuda()[:, None, :].expand(-1, H, -1)]
                assert (s - 1).abs().max() < 2e-2, s
            logp = torch.log_softmax(o.logits.float(), -1)
            pent = -(logp.exp() * logp).sum(-1)  # predictive entropy per position (B, T2)

        for j, qi in enumerate(idx):
            P, m, n = len(batch[j]), len(gens[j]), len(full[j])
            off = T2 - n
            rec = dict(qs[qi], answer=tok.decode(gens[j], skip_special_tokens=True).strip(),
                       n_prompt=P, n_answer=m, order=int(qi))
            if m == 0:
                for k in feats:
                    feats[k].append(np.full((L, H), np.nan, dtype=np.float32))
                records.append(rec)
                continue
            pos = torch.arange(P - 1, P + m - 1, device=ent.device)  # unpadded positions producing answer tokens
            e = ent[:, j, :, off + pos]                               # (L, H, m)
            ne = e / torch.log((pos + 1).float())                     # row at position p attends to p+1 tokens
            feats["ent_ans"].append(e.mean(-1).cpu().numpy())
            feats["ent_first"].append(e[..., 0].cpu().numpy())
            feats["nent_ans"].append(ne.mean(-1).cpu().numpy())
            feats["nent_first"].append(ne[..., 0].cpu().numpy())
            tgt = torch.tensor(gens[j], device=ent.device)
            nll = -logp[j, off + pos, tgt]
            pe = pent[j, off + pos]
            rec.update(nll_mean=nll.mean().item(), nll_max=nll.max().item(), nll_first=nll[0].item(),
                       pent_mean=pe.mean().item(), pent_max=pe.max().item(), pent_first=pe[0].item())
            records.append(rec)
        del o, ent, logp, pent

    inv = np.argsort([r["order"] for r in records])
    records = [records[i] for i in inv]
    with open(f"results/model_outputs/{args.tag}.jsonl", "w") as f:
        for r in records:
            f.write(json.dumps(r, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    np.savez_compressed(f"results/features/{args.tag}.npz",
                        **{k: np.stack(v)[inv].astype(np.float16) for k, v in feats.items()})
    print(f"done {len(records)} examples in {time.time() - t0:.0f}s; "
          f"empty answers: {sum(r['n_answer'] == 0 for r in records)}", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
EOF

"""Label each generated answer as correct / incorrect (hallucinated) / abstain.

Two labels are written to results/evaluations/<tag>_labels.jsonl:
  judge  : reference-based LLM judge (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, greedy) - primary label
  strmatch: 1 if any normalized gold alias is contained in the normalized answer
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import re
import string
import unicodedata

import torch
from tqdm import tqdm
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

JUDGE_SYSTEM = "You are a strict but fair grader of short factual answers."
JUDGE_TEMPLATE = """Question: {question}
Reference answer(s): {gold}
Model answer: {answer}

Grade the model answer against the reference answer(s).
- CORRECT: it states the same fact as at least one reference answer (different wording, spelling variants, extra non-contradictory detail, or a more specific answer that implies the reference are all fine).
- INCORRECT: it states a different fact, or is too vague/general to match the reference.
- ABSTAIN: it declines to answer or says it does not know.
Reply with exactly one word: CORRECT, INCORRECT, or ABSTAIN."""


def normalize(s):
    """SQuAD-style normalization plus accent stripping."""
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", s.lower())
    s = "".join(c for c in s if not unicodedata.combining(c))
    s = "".join(c if c not in string.punctuation else " " for c in s)
    s = re.sub(r"\b(a|an|the)\b", " ", s)
    return " ".join(s.split())


def string_match(answer, gold):
    a = normalize(answer)
    return int(any(g and re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(g)}\b", a) for g in map(normalize, gold)))


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--tags", nargs="+", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--judge", default="Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct")
    ap.add_argument("--batch_size", type=int, default=48)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(args.judge)
    tok.padding_side = "left"
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(args.judge, dtype=torch.bfloat16).cuda().eval()
    os.makedirs("results/evaluations", exist_ok=True)

    for tag in args.tags:
        recs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(f"results/model_outputs/{tag}.jsonl")]
        prompts = [tok.apply_chat_template(
            [{"role": "system", "content": JUDGE_SYSTEM},
             {"role": "user", "content": JUDGE_TEMPLATE.format(
                 question=r["question"], gold=" | ".join(r["gold"][:12]), answer=r["answer"] or "(empty)")}],
            tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) for r in recs]
        order = sorted(range(len(prompts)), key=lambda i: len(prompts[i]))
        verdicts = [None] * len(recs)
        for b in tqdm(range(0, len(order), args.batch_size), mininterval=30):
            idx = order[b: b + args.batch_size]
            enc = tok([prompts[i] for i in idx], return_tensors="pt", padding=True,
                      add_special_tokens=False).to("cuda")
            with torch.no_grad():
                out = model.generate(**enc, do_sample=False, max_new_tokens=4, pad_token_id=tok.pad_token_id)
            for i, o in zip(idx, out):
                v = tok.decode(o[enc.input_ids.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True).strip().upper()
                verdicts[i] = ("INCORRECT" if v.startswith("INCORRECT") else "CORRECT" if v.startswith("CORRECT")
                               else "ABSTAIN" if v.startswith("ABSTAIN") else "UNPARSED:" + v)
        with open(f"results/evaluations/{tag}_labels.jsonl", "w") as f:
            for r, v in zip(recs, verdicts):
                f.write(json.dumps(dict(qid=r["qid"], judge=v, strmatch=string_match(r["answer"], r["gold"]))) + "\n")
        from collections import Counter
        print(tag, Counter(verdicts), "strmatch acc", sum(string_match(r["answer"], r["gold"]) for r in recs) / len(recs))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-25919/bundled-skills/2.1.293/1211b5dd5e47715dbabd88c7e5195337/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #ffffff;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the

"""Statistical analysis for the attention-entropy hallucination study.

Usage: python src/analyze.py --tag qwen25_7b [--label judge|strmatch]
Writes results/analysis/<tag>[_strmatch].json and CSV tables next to it.
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedStratifiedKFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

SEED = 42
DOMAINS = ["biography", "geography", "creative_works", "science", "trivia"]
LOGIT_COLS = ["nll_mean", "nll_max", "nll_first", "pent_mean", "pent_max", "pent_first"]


def load(tag, label="judge"):
    """Return (df, feats) restricted to answered, gradable examples. y=1 means hallucinated."""
    df = pd.DataFrame([json.loads(l) for l in open(f"results/model_outputs/{tag}.jsonl")])
    lab = pd.DataFrame([json.loads(l) for l in open(f"results/evaluations/{tag}_labels.jsonl")])
    assert (df.qid.values == lab.qid.values).all()
    df["judge"], df["strmatch"] = lab.judge.values, lab.strmatch.values
    npz = np.load(f"results/features/{tag}.npz")
    feats = {k: npz[k].astype(np.float64) for k in npz.files}
    # Abstentions are defined by the judge under both labelings, so both use the same examples.
    keep = (df.n_answer > 0) & df.judge.isin(["CORRECT", "INCORRECT"])
    counts = dict(total=len(df), empty=int((df.n_answer == 0).sum()),
                  abstain=int((df.judge == "ABSTAIN").sum()),
                  unparsed=int(df.judge.str.startswith("UNPARSED").sum()), kept=int(keep.sum()))
    df["y"] = (df.judge == "INCORRECT").astype(int) if label == "judge" else 1 - df.strmatch
    idx = np.where(keep.values)[0]
    df = df.iloc[idx].reset_index(drop=True)
    feats = {k: v[idx] for k, v in feats.items()}
    assert not any(np.isnan(v).any() for v in feats.values())
    return df, feats, counts


def boot_ci(fn, n, B, rng, strata=None):
    """Percentile bootstrap CI of fn(indices); resamples within strata if given."""
    groups = [np.arange(n)] if strata is None else [np.where(strata == s)[0] for s in np.unique(strata)]
    vals = []
    for _ in range(B):
        ii = np.concatenate([rng.choice(g, len(g)) for g in groups])
        vals.append(fn(ii))
    return np.percentile(vals, [2.5, 97.5]).tolist(), np.asarray(vals)


def cohens_d(a, b):
    sp = np.sqrt(((len(a) - 1) * a.var(ddof=1) + (len(b) - 1) * b.var(ddof=1)) / (len(a) + len(b) - 2))
    return float((a.mean() - b.mean()) / sp)


def effect(x, y, rng, B=10000):
    """Hallucinated-vs-factual comparison of a scalar x. Bootstrap is stratified by class."""
    h, f = x[y == 1], x[y == 0]
    rel = lambda ii: (x[ii][y[ii] == 1].mean() / x[ii][y[ii] == 0].mean() - 1) * 100
    ci, _ = boot_ci(rel, len(x), B, rng, strata=y)
    return dict(n_halluc=int(len(h)), n_factual=int(len(f)), mean_halluc=float(h.mean()),
                mean_factual=float(f.mean()), rel_diff_pct=float((h.mean() / f.mean() - 1) * 100),
                rel_diff_ci95=ci, cohens_d=cohens_d(h, f),
                mwu_p=float(stats.mannwhitneyu(h, f, alternative="two-sided").pvalue),
                auroc_single=float(roc_auc_score(y, x)))


def clf():
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=3000))


def cv_scores(X, y, n_rep=5):
    """Out-of-fold decision scores averaged over repeats, plus the per-repeat AUROCs."""
    X = X.reshape(len(X), -1)
    oof = np.zeros((n_rep, len(y)))
    rskf = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=n_rep, random_state=SEED)
    for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(rskf.split(X, y)):
        oof[k // 5, te] = clf().fit(X[tr], y[tr]).decision_function(X[te])
    rep_auc = [roc_auc_score(y, o) for o in oof]
    return oof.mean(0), rep_auc


def auc_report(score, y, rng, rep_auc=None, B=2000):
    ci, vals = boot_ci(lambda ii: roc_auc_score(y[ii], score[ii]), len(y), B, rng, strata=y)
    out = dict(auroc=float(roc_auc_score(y, score)), ci95=ci, auprc=float(average_precision_score(y, score)),
               n=int(len(y)), halluc_rate=float(y.mean()))
    if rep_auc is not None:
        out["repeat_mean"], out["repeat_sd"] = float(np.mean(rep_auc)), float(np.std(rep_auc, ddof=1))
    return out, vals


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--tag", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--label", default="judge", choices=["judge", "strmatch"])
    ap.add_argument("--fast", action="store_true", help="skip per-head model and transfer matrix")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    df, F, counts = load(args.tag, args.label)
    y, dom = df.y.values, df.domain.values
    L = F["ent_ans"].shape[1]
    res = dict(tag=args.tag, label=args.label, counts=counts, n_layers=L, n_heads=F["ent_ans"].shape[2])
    out_dir = "results/analysis"
    os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)
    sfx = "" if args.label == "judge" else "_strmatch"

    res["by_domain_base"] = {d: dict(n=int((dom == d).sum()), halluc_rate=float(y[dom == d].mean()),
                                     n_prompt=float(df.n_prompt[dom == d].mean()),
                                     n_answer=float(df.n_answer[dom == d].mean())) for d in DOMAINS}
    lab_all = pd.DataFrame([json.loads(l) for l in open(f"results/evaluations/{args.tag}_labels.jsonl")])
    gr = lab_all[lab_all.judge.isin(["CORRECT", "INCORRECT"])]
    res["judge_strmatch_agreement"] = float(((gr.judge == "CORRECT").astype(int) == gr.strmatch).mean())

    # Layer-level features: mean over heads.
    lay = {k: v.mean(2) for k, v in F.items()}  # (N, L)
    last3 = {k: v[:, -3:].mean(1) for k, v in lay.items()}
    logn_p, logn_a = np.log(df.n_prompt.values), np.log(df.n_answer.values)

    # ---------------- E1: effect size ----------------
    e1 = {}
    for k in ["ent_ans", "ent_first", "nent_ans", "nent_first"]:
        e1[k] = dict(pooled=effect(last3[k], y, rng))
        for d in DOMAINS:
            m = dom == d
            e1[k][d] = effect(last3[k][m], y[m], rng, B=4000)
        e1[k]["macro_domain_rel_diff_pct"] = float(np.mean([e1[k][d]["rel_diff_pct"] for d in DOMAINS]))
    # Adjusted difference: OLS with domain fixed effects and length covariates (HC3 SEs).
    d_ols = pd.DataFrame(dict(x=last3["ent_ans"], y=y, lp=logn_p, la=logn_a, dom=dom))
    for name, formula in [("domain_FE", "x ~ y + C(dom)"), ("domain_FE_plus_length", "x ~ y + C(dom) + lp + la")]:
        fit = smf.ols(formula, d_ols).fit(cov_type="HC3")
        base = d_ols.x[d_ols.y == 0].mean()
        lo, hi = fit.conf_int().loc["y"]
        e1[f"ols_{name}"] = dict(coef_nats=float(fit.params["y"]), pct_of_factual_mean=float(fit.params["y"] / base * 100),
                                 ci95_pct=[float(lo / base * 100), float(hi / base * 100)], p=float(fit.pvalues["y"]))
    res["E1_last3_effect"] = e1

    # Per-layer profile with BH-FDR over layers.
    rows = []
    for k in ["ent_ans", "ent_first"]:
        for l in range(L):
            x = lay[k][:, l]
            h, f = x[y == 1], x[y == 0]
            rows.append(dict(feature=k, layer=l, mean_halluc=h.mean(), mean_factual=f.mean(),
                             rel_diff_pct=(h.mean() / f.mean() - 1) * 100, cohens_d=cohens_d(h, f),
                             d_within_domain=float(np.mean([cohens_d(x[(y == 1) & (dom == d)], x[(y == 0) & (dom == d)])
                                                            for d in DOMAINS])),
                             p=stats.mannwhitneyu(h, f).pvalue))
    pl = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    pl["p_fdr"] = np.concatenate([multipletests(g.p, method="fdr_bh")[1] for _, g in pl.groupby("feature", sort=False)])
    pl.to_csv(f"{out_dir}/{args.tag}{sfx}_per_layer.csv", index=False)
    res["per_layer_n_sig_fdr"] = {k: int((g.p_fdr < 0.05).sum()) for k, g in pl.groupby("feature")}

    # ---------------- E2/E4: classifiers (pooled) ----------------
    length = np.c_[logn_p, logn_a]
    logit = df[LOGIT_COLS].values
    dom_oh = pd.get_dummies(df.domain).values.astype(float)
    sets = {
        "domain_only": dom_oh,
        "length_only": length,
        "entropy_last3_mean (1 feat)": last3["ent_ans"][:, None],
        "entropy_layers (ans mean)": lay["ent_ans"],
        "entropy_layers (first token)": lay["ent_first"],
        "norm_entropy_layers (ans mean)": lay["nent_ans"],
        "entropy_layers + length": np.c_[lay["ent_ans"], length],
        "logit_baseline": logit,
        "nll_mean only": df[["nll_mean"]].values,
        "entropy_layers + logit": np.c_[lay["ent_ans"], logit],
    }
    if not args.fast:
        sets["entropy_heads (L*H)"] = F["ent_ans"]
    e2, oof = {}, {}
    for name, X in sets.items():
        s, rep = cv_scores(X, y)
        oof[name] = s
        e2[name], _ = auc_report(s, y, rng, rep)
        # AUROC of the pooled model's scores inside each domain (removes between-domain base-rate signal).
        e2[name]["within_domain_macro_auroc"] = float(np.mean([roc_auc_score(y[dom == d], s[dom == d]) for d in DOMAINS]))
        print(f"{name:34s} AUROC {e2[name]['auroc']:.3f} {np.round(e2[name]['ci95'], 3)} "
              f"within-domain macro {e2[name]['within_domain_macro_auroc']:.3f}", flush=True)
    res["E2_pooled_classifiers"] = e2
    # Paired bootstrap: does adding entropy to logits help? does entropy beat length?
    def paired(a, b, B=2000):
        ci, v = boot_ci(lambda ii: roc_auc_score(y[ii], oof[a][ii]) - roc_auc_score(y[ii], oof[b][ii]), len(y), B, rng, strata=y)
        return dict(diff=float(roc_auc_score(y, oof[a]) - roc_auc_score(y, oof[b])), ci95=ci, p_two_sided=float(min(1, 2 * min((v <= 0).mean(), (v >= 0).mean()))))
    res["E4_paired"] = {
        "entropy_layers - length_only": paired("entropy_layers (ans mean)", "length_only"),
        "entropy_layers - domain_only": paired("entropy_layers (ans mean)", "domain_only"),
        "entropy_layers - logit_baseline": paired("entropy_layers (ans mean)", "logit_baseline"),
        "entropy+logit - logit_baseline": paired("entropy_layers + logit", "logit_baseline"),
    }

    # ---------------- E3: per-domain ----------------
    e3, boots = {}, {}
    for d in DOMAINS:
        m = dom == d
        e3[d] = {}
        for name in ["entropy_layers (ans mean)", "entropy_layers (first token)", "norm_entropy_layers (ans mean)",
                     "length_only", "logit_baseline", "entropy_layers + logit"]:
            s, rep = cv_scores(sets[name][m], y[m])
            e3[d][name], v = auc_report(s, y[m], rng, rep)
            if name == "entropy_layers (ans mean)":
                boots[d] = v
    res["E3_within_domain"] = e3
    key = "entropy_layers (ans mean)"
    order = sorted(DOMAINS, key=lambda d: -e3[d][key]["auroc"])
    diff = boots["biography"] - boots["science"]
    res["E3_ordering"] = dict(
        ranking_high_to_low=order,
        bio_minus_science=dict(diff=e3["biography"][key]["auroc"] - e3["science"][key]["auroc"],
                               ci95=np.percentile(diff, [2.5, 97.5]).tolist(),
                               p_two_sided=float(min(1, 2 * min((diff <= 0).mean(), (diff >= 0).mean())))),
        # Bootstrap probability that biography is the top domain and science the bottom one.
        p_boot_bio_highest=float(np.mean(np.argmax(np.c_[[boots[d] for d in DOMAINS]], 0) == DOMAINS.index("biography"))),
        p_boot_science_lowest=float(np.mean(np.argmin(np.c_[[boots[d] for d in DOMAINS]], 0) == DOMAINS.index("science"))))
    if not args.fast:
        T = np.zeros((5, 5))
        for i, a in enumerate(DOMAINS):
            for j, b in enumerate(DOMAINS):
                if i == j:
                    T[i, j] = e3[a][key]["auroc"]
                else:
                    T[i, j] = roc_auc_score(y[dom == b], clf().fit(lay["ent_ans"][dom == a], y[dom == a])
                                            .decision_function(lay["ent_ans"][dom == b]))
        pd.DataFrame(T, index=DOMAINS, columns=DOMAINS).to_csv(f"{out_dir}/{args.tag}{sfx}_transfer.csv")
        res["E3_transfer_offdiag_mean"] = float(T[~np.eye(5, dtype=bool)].mean())
        # PopQA-relation breakdown (error analysis): pooled-model scores within each relation.
        rel = []
        for r, g in df[df.source == "PopQA"].groupby("relation"):
            if g.y.nunique() == 2 and g.y.value_counts().min() >= 20:
                rel.append(dict(relation=r, domain=g.domain.iloc[0], n=len(g), halluc_rate=g.y.mean(),
                                auroc_entropy=roc_auc_score(g.y, oof[key][g.index]),
                                auroc_logit=roc_auc_score(g.y, oof["logit_baseline"][g.index])))
        pd.DataFrame(rel).to_csv(f"{out_dir}/{args.tag}{sfx}_by_relation.csv", index=False)

    # Save per-example scores for figures / error analysis.
    out = df[["qid", "domain", "relation", "question", "answer", "y", "n_prompt", "n_answer", "nll_mean"]].copy()
    out["ent_last3"] = last3["ent_ans"]
    out["score_entropy"] = oof[key]
    out["score_logit"] = oof["logit_baseline"]
    out.to_csv(f"{out_dir}/{args.tag}{sfx}_examples.csv", index=False)
    np.save(f"{out_dir}/{args.tag}{sfx}_layer_ent.npy", lay["ent_ans"])
    json.dump(res, open(f"{out_dir}/{args.tag}{sfx}.json", "w"), indent=1)
    print(json.dumps({k: res[k] for k in ["counts", "by_domain_base", "judge_strmatch_agreement", "E3_ordering", "E4_paired"]}, indent=1))
    print(json.dumps({k: {kk: (round(vv["rel_diff_pct"], 2), np.round(vv["rel_diff_ci95"], 2).tolist(), round(vv["cohens_d"], 3))
                          for kk, vv in v.items() if isinstance(vv, dict)} for k, v in e1.items() if not k.startswith("ols")}, indent=1))
    print({k: v for k, v in e1.items() if k.startswith("ols")})
    print({d: (round(e3[d][key]["auroc"], 3), np.round(e3[d][key]["ci95"], 3).tolist()) for d in DOMAINS})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Usage: python src/analyze.py --tag qwen25_7b [--label judge|strmatch]
Writes results/analysis/<tag>[_strmatch].json and CSV tables next to it.

import json
import os
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
